segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jude, a slave of Jesus Christ and brother of James, to those who are called, loved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: May mercy, peace and love be multiplied to you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Beloved, while I was making every effort to write to you about the salvation we share, I found it necessary to write and urge you to contend for the faith that was handed down once for all to the holy ones.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For certain people have slipped in unnoticed, people long ago written down for this condemnation, ungodly people who turn the grace of our God into debauchery and deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now I want to remind you, though you have come to know all this once for all, that Jesus, having saved a people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and the angels who did not keep their own domain but abandoned their proper dwelling he has kept in everlasting chains beneath the gloom for the judgment of the great day;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: just as Sodom and Gomorrah and the towns around them, having in the same way as these given themselves to sexual immorality and gone after flesh of another kind, lie on display as an example, undergoing the punishment of eternal fire.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Yet in the same way these people also, dreaming as they do, defile the flesh, reject authority, and slander the glorious ones.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Michael the archangel, when he was disputing with the devil and arguing about the body of Moses, did not dare to bring a slanderous judgment against him, but said,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “May the Lord rebuke you!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But these people slander whatever they do not understand, and what they do know by instinct, like unreasoning animals—by these things they are destroyed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Woe to them! For they have gone the way of Cain, abandoned themselves for pay to Balaam’s error, and perished in Korah’s rebellion.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: These are the ones who are hidden reefs at your love-feasts, feasting with you, shepherding themselves without fear; waterless clouds carried along by winds; late-autumn trees without fruit, twice dead, uprooted;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: wild waves of the sea, foaming up their own shameful deeds; wandering stars, for whom the gloom of darkness has been kept forever.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It was also about these people that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Look, the Lord has come with his holy myriads,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: to execute judgment on all and to convict all the ungodly of all the ungodly deeds they have done in their ungodliness, and of all the harsh things that ungodly sinners have spoken against him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: These are grumblers, complainers about their lot, following their own desires; their mouths speak bombast, and they flatter people for the sake of gain.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But you, beloved, remember the words spoken beforehand by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: how they used to say to you,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “In the last time there will be scoffers, following their own ungodly desires.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: These are the ones who cause divisions, merely natural people who do not have the Spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But you, beloved, building yourselves up on your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Spirit,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: keep yourselves in the love of God, waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And have mercy on some, who are wavering;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: save others, snatching them out of the fire; and on others have mercy with fear, hating even the tunic stained by the flesh.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now to the one who is able to guard you from stumbling and to set you before his glory without blemish and with exultation,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to the only God our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, belong glory, majesty, might and authority, before every age, now, and for all the ages. Amen.

notes.note: The Greek word meant a person owned by another, and first-century hearers understood it that way. Many translations use 'servant' or 'bondservant', partly to avoid association with modern race-based slavery; several recent ones use 'slave'. In Jewish usage 'slave of God' could also be a title of honour for one wholly at his master's disposal.

The writer's name in Greek is Judas (Hebrew Judah); English tradition uses 'Jude' to distinguish him from Judas Iscariot. The James meant is almost certainly the well-known leader of the Jerusalem church, which would make this Jude one of the brothers of Jesus named in the Gospels, though he does not claim that relationship himself.

notes.traditional: kept for Jesus Christ / preserved in Jesus Christ
notes.note: The Greek dative can mean 'kept for Jesus Christ' (until his coming) or 'kept by Jesus Christ'. Most recent translations choose 'for', as here. The verb 'keep' recurs through the letter (verses 6, 13, 21) and is rendered the same way each time.

'Saints' now suggests an exceptional class of canonised individuals. The Greek word is the ordinary term, taken from the Greek Old Testament, for the whole people set apart as God's own, here all believers.

notes.phrase: our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ
notes.traditional: our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ
notes.note: A single Greek article governs 'Master' and 'Lord', so most scholars take both titles as referring to Jesus Christ. The phrase can also be read as 'the only Master, and our Lord Jesus Christ', with 'Master' referring to God; some later manuscripts add 'God' to make that explicit.

The manuscripts are divided: some read 'Jesus', others 'the Lord', and a few 'God' or 'God Christ'. The edition translated here, like the most recent critical editions, reads 'Jesus', as the harder reading with strong early support; many English versions follow the manuscripts that read 'the Lord'. On this reading Jude credits the pre-existent Jesus with the exodus and the judgment in the wilderness (Numbers 14).

notes.phrase: the angels who did not keep their own domain
notes.traditional: kept not their first estate / did not stay within their own position of authority
notes.note: Jude alludes to a widely known Jewish reading of Genesis 6:1–4, developed at length in the book of 1 Enoch, in which angels left heaven to take human wives and were bound in darkness until the day of judgment. The word rendered 'domain' means a sphere of rule or assigned office. 'Everlasting' here translates a different Greek word from the one rendered 'eternal' in verses 7 and 21.

The Greek is literally 'other flesh', with a word for 'other' that usually implies difference in kind. Since 'these' most naturally refers back to the angels of verse 6, many scholars think the point is that the men of Sodom sought intercourse with angels (Genesis 19), mirroring angels who sought human women. Others take the phrase as a reference to same-sex relations, and some take 'these' as Sodom and Gomorrah themselves.

The word is formed from 'age' and in Jewish usage often refers to what belongs to the age to come, so it describes kind as well as duration. 'Eternal life' in verse 21 is the life of that coming age. A minority of translators render it 'of the age to come' throughout.

In ordinary Greek the verb meant to speak abusively of anyone, human or divine; English 'blaspheme' narrows it to speech against God. 'Slander' is used here and in verses 9 and 10 so that the repeated word stays visible. Translations vary between 'blaspheme', 'revile' and 'slander'.

Literally 'glories'. Most scholars take this as a term for angelic beings, which fits the example of Michael that follows; older versions understood it as human dignitaries. 'Authority' just before it is literally 'lordship' and may refer to the authority of the Lord himself.

notes.traditional: a railing accusation / a blasphemous judgment
notes.note: The Greek, literally 'a judgment of slander', can mean an abusive verdict or a verdict convicting the devil of slander; in either case Michael leaves the judgment to God. The story of a dispute over Moses's body is not in the Old Testament; early Christian writers say it came from a Jewish work about Moses's death whose ending is now lost. Michael's words echo Zechariah 3:2.

Three Old Testament figures serve as types: Cain, who murdered his brother (Genesis 4); Balaam, who in Jewish tradition led Israel into sin for the sake of payment (Numbers 22–25; 31:16); and Korah, who led a revolt against Moses and was swallowed by the earth (Numbers 16). The past tenses treat the opponents' fate as already sealed.

In Greek of the period this word normally means a rock or reef in the sea, a hidden danger to ships. Some translations render 'blemishes' or 'stains', taking it as equivalent to a similar word used in the parallel at 2 Peter 2:13; that sense is attested only later. The 'love-feasts' were the shared meals of the early Christian assemblies, with which the Lord's Supper was associated.

The quotation corresponds to 1 Enoch 1:9, from a Jewish work widely read in the period and attributed to the Enoch of Genesis 5, seventh in the line from Adam counting inclusively. The Greek verb is a past tense, used as prophets often did to present a future event as already accomplished. Most translations smooth this to 'comes' or 'is coming'.

The adjective comes from the word for 'soul' or natural life and describes people operating on the level of ordinary human life alone, in contrast to those who have the Spirit (compare 1 Corinthians 2:14). 'Sensual' wrongly suggests bodily indulgence, and 'worldly' is looser than the Greek. 'Spirit' could be read as the human spirit, but most scholars take it as God's Spirit.

notes.phrase: have mercy on some, who are wavering
notes.traditional: have mercy on those who doubt
notes.note: The text of verses 22–23 is among the most uncertain in the New Testament: manuscripts give two groups or three, and some read 'convict' or 'refute' in place of the first 'have mercy'. The three-group form translated here is the one most editions print. The participle rendered 'wavering' is the same verb translated 'disputing' in verse 9, so the sense may instead be 'those who dispute'.
